title: What's the Secret to Your Hardest Job?
author: The Daily Dad
summary: The Daily Dad reflects on the paradox that parenting is universally recognized as the world's hardest job, yet it comes with no training, no clear job description, and no fixed outcomes. Rather than prescribe specific behaviors, the essay draws on Epictetus's response to a struggling student: instead of asking 'what should I do?', ask for the capacity to 'adapt to any circumstance.' The implication for parenting is that the secret is not finding the right rules or book but developing general principles and inner resilience that flex in response to the unpredictable flow of family life. Parenting is framed as river-rafting: keeping the boat upright through ever-changing circumstances. The secret is a posture -- studied, principled, and adaptable -- rather than a technique.
points: * Parenting is the hardest job because it layers on top of all other jobs, cannot be quit or retired from, has no clear job description, and offers no pay. * Epictetus advised a struggling student against asking 'tell me what to do' -- the better request is to 'make me adaptable to any circumstance.' * The secret to parenting is not memorizing the right rules but developing general principles that allow flexible, wise response to unpredictable situations. * Parenting is like river-rafting: 'navigating a seemingly unending, ever-changing flow of complicated circumstances, dilemma after dilemma, new situation after new situation, trying not to let the boat flip.' * Training and readiness are essential: 'You must train to be able to respond. To keep the bow in front of the stern, and everything upright. You must be ready for it all.' * Epictetus: 'There may be events that call for you to act differently... So hold on to general principles and you won't need specific advice.'
quotes: It's not just a job. It's the job that you have to do on top of your other jobs. It's the one job you can't quit or get promoted or retire from.
Epictetus told him that he would not. This wasn't even the right request, he said. It would be far better to ask a teacher to 'make me adaptable to any circumstance.'
'There may be events that call for you to act differently... So hold on to general principles and you won't need specific advice.'

Like rafting a river, it is navigating a seemingly unending, ever-changing flow of complicated circumstances, dilemma after dilemma, new situation after new situation, trying not to let the boat flip.
You must train to be able to respond. To keep the bow in front of the stern, and everything upright. You must be ready for it all.
